title: Mixed numbers and improper fractions
keyIdea: An improper fraction has a numerator bigger than (or equal to) its denominator, so it is worth 1 or more, like 11/4. A mixed number writes the same amount as a whole number and a proper fraction, like 2 3/4. To convert 11/4, find how many groups of 4 fit in 11 (2, remainder 3): 2 3/4. To go back, multiply the wholes by the denominator and add the numerator: 3 2/5 = (3 × 5 + 2)/5 = 17/5.

kid: A fraction can be more than 1. Think of a bar cut into 4 equal parts. Each part is a quarter. 4 quarters fill the bar, so 4/4 is 1 whole. If you have 7 quarters, the first bar fills up and 3 quarters go into a second bar.

We can write that amount in two ways. 7/4 is an improper fraction. Its top number, the numerator, is bigger than its bottom number, the denominator. 1 3/4 is a mixed number. It is a whole number and a fraction side by side. Both name the same amount.

To turn an improper fraction into a mixed number, make as many wholes as you can. For 11/4, groups of 4 fit into 11 two times, with 3 left. So 11/4 is 2 3/4. This is just division with a remainder: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 r 3.

To go the other way, break every whole into pieces. In 3 2/5, each whole is 5 fifths, so 3 wholes are 15 fifths. Add the 2 fifths and you get 17 fifths, or 17/5. Wholes times the denominator, then add the numerator.
adult: This is the England National Curriculum Year 5 statement: recognise mixed numbers and improper fractions, convert from one form to the other, and write statements greater than 1 as a mixed number (for example 2/5 + 4/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5). The US Common Core builds the same idea in 4.NF.B.3, where fractions are sums of unit fractions. The key fact is that n/n = 1, so every group of d pieces of size 1/d is one whole.

A common mistake is the belief that a fraction must be less than 1, so 7/4 looks impossible or gets placed between 0 and 1 on a number line. Others read the digits instead of the quantity, so 11/4 becomes 1 1/4. When converting back, children often add all the numbers (3 2/5 becomes 5/5) or drop the whole part entirely. Each slip shows the child is not yet thinking of the whole as d pieces of size 1/d.

The lab keeps the bar model in view the whole time. Your child pours quarters into bars and watches 7/4 spill into a second bar. Then they bundle 11 quarters into wholes, cut the 3 wholes of 3 2/5 into fifths and count all 17 pieces. They build targets piece by piece and place 9/4 and 2 1/2 on a number line.

Only teach the shortcut (multiply and add, or divide and keep the remainder) once the pictures make sense. Then ask your child why it works. A good answer is: each whole is worth the denominator in pieces.

familyTip: Cut toast or a chocolate bar into quarters and share out 9 pieces between plates that each hold 4. Ask how many full plates and how many extra quarters there are, then write it both ways: 9/4 and 2 1/4.

visual.caption: Proper fraction, improper fraction or mixed number? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: pour quarters past a whole, bundle 11/4, cut 3 2/5 into fifths and place 9/4 on a number line.

practice.prompt: Which of these is an improper fraction?
practice.hint: Look for a numerator that is as big as or bigger than the denominator.
practice.explain: 8/5 has 8 on top and 5 underneath, so it is more than 1 whole. 5/8 is less than 1, and 1 3/5 is a mixed number.

practice.prompt: A mixed number has {w} wholes and 1/{d} more. How many pieces of size 1/{d} is that in total? (Write the numerator of the improper fraction.)
practice.hint: Each whole is {d} pieces. Multiply the wholes by {d}, then add the extra 1.
practice.explain: {w} × {d} = {=w*d} pieces in the wholes, plus 1 more makes {=w*d+1}. So the improper fraction is {=w*d+1}/{d}.

practice.prompt: Write {n}/4 as a mixed number. How many wholes does it have?
practice.hint: How many groups of 4 fit into {n}? The remainder becomes the fraction part.

practice.prompt: Ella says 3 2/5 = 5/5 because 3 + 2 = 5. What went wrong?
choices: Each whole is 5 fifths, so she needed 3 × 5 + 2 = 17
practice.hint: How many fifths are in just one whole?
practice.explain: One whole is 5 fifths, so 3 wholes are 15 fifths. With the extra 2 fifths, 3 2/5 = 17/5. Adding 3 + 2 treats wholes and fifths as the same size.

pool.prompt: What is 11/4 as a mixed number?
pool.hint: How many groups of 4 fit in 11, and what is left over?
pool.explain: 11 ÷ 4 = 2 remainder 3. So 11/4 = 2 3/4. Reading the digits as 1 1/4 is a common slip.

pool.hint: Turn each whole into fifths first.
pool.explain: 2 wholes are 10 fifths. Add 3 fifths to get 13/5.

pool.prompt: Where does 7/4 go on a number line?
pool.hint: Is 7 quarters more or less than 4 quarters?
pool.explain: 4 quarters make 1, and 8 quarters make 2. 7 quarters is between them, so 7/4 = 1 3/4 sits between 1 and 2.

pool.prompt: How many thirds are in {w} wholes?
pool.hint: 1 whole is cut into 3 thirds, so count 3 for every whole.
pool.explain: Each whole is 3 thirds, so {w} wholes are {w} × 3 = {=w*3} thirds. That is {=w*3}/3.

pool.hint: Fifths add to fifths, then check if you have more than 5 of them.
pool.explain: 2 fifths and 4 fifths make 6 fifths. That is 1 whole (5 fifths) and 1 fifth more, so 6/5 = 1 1/5.

pool.prompt: What is 12/4 written as a whole number?
pool.hint: How many groups of 4 quarters can you make from 12?
pool.explain: 12 quarters make exactly 3 groups of 4, so 12/4 = 3 with nothing left over.

pool.prompt: A pizza is cut into 8 slices. You eat {n} slices from a pile of pizzas. Write {n}/8 as a mixed number. How many slices are in the fraction part?
pool.hint: Take away full pizzas of 8 slices until fewer than 8 are left.
pool.explain: {n} ÷ 8 = {=(n-n%8)/8} remainder {=n%8}, so there are {=n%8} slices, or {=n%8}/8, in the fraction part.

pool.hint: Change everything to quarters: 2 is 8 quarters.
pool.explain: 2 = 8/4, so 9/4 is biggest. 9/4 = 2 1/4, a quarter more than 2.

pool.prompt: Sam turns 4 1/3 into 4/3. What did he forget?
choices: The 4 wholes are 12 thirds, so it should be 13/3
pool.explain: 4/3 is only 1 1/3. The 4 wholes are 4 × 3 = 12 thirds; add 1 third to get 13/3.
